subtopic: NECESSITY OF WAYS AND MEANS MOTION
NECESSITY OF WAYS AND MEANS MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday at this point, I rose on a point of order after the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) gave notice of a Ways and Means motion relating to the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States. It is my understanding that the Government wishes to seek the concurrence of the House now in that Ways and Means motion before we go on to the important Meech Lake debate later this morning.
I am of course, Mr. Speaker, making an assumption that you will be making a ruling on my point of order in advance of the question being put to the House, and I wish to take a moment to make some additional comments to clarify the point of order I raised yesterday.
As you will recall, the thrust of my objection to the Ways and Means motion rested on two fundamental points: first, that because the Ways and Means motion contained no provision to increase charges to the public, it was therefore totally unnecessary as a preliminary step to the introduction of the free trade legislation. I cited a number of authorities, including Beauchesne and Erskine May, to corroborate my point. Second, I argued that by its very nature, a Ways and Means motion limits the scope for amendments to the Bill that it precedes, and Beauchesne is absolutely clear on this point.
In your preliminary response that you made yesterday to my intervention, you indicated that, without seeing the Bill, it was difficult to determine whether it would impose an additional charge on the taxpayer. You stated, as reported in Hansard at page 15587:
The second matter of course is that without seeing the Bill I am not completely sure that 1 would be able to accept some of the propositions which the Hon. Member has cited, which may of themselves be good authority. However, I cannot tell until I see the Bill whether in fact the Bill conforms with the five paragraphs that are now in front of the House and the notice of Ways and Means motion. I draw to the attention of the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap the fact that paragraph i) of the notice of Ways and Means motion states:
i) to impose customs duties in accordance with the Tariff Schedules of
Canada referred to in Annex 401.2 of the Agreement;
I cannot tell from that whether that will increase customs duties or decrease them. It seems to me it puts us in some difficulty.
I recognize your difficulty, Mr. Speaker. However, consider the implications on Members of the House from all sides who participate in the legislative process of giving the Government a carte blanche opportunity to introduce Ways and Means motions. Consider, for example, the following case that could arise out of the ability of a Government to introduce Ways and Means to any Bill where charges on the taxpayer are altered, either to increase charges or to decrease them.
Let us consider the possibility of a Ways and Means motion being sufficiently vague and obscure as to leave some doubt in the minds of Members of the House about whether they are voting on whether or not to concur in a motion that would
May 19, 1988

result in increased taxes or in decreased taxes on the general public, their constituents. How can Members make a decision on a question which is not clear? Surely that is fundamental to this place. Members of Parliament must know what they are voting on before they can decide how they will vote. On a fundamental issue such as taxation, the importance of this question is heightened even further.
If the motion is unclear, how should I vote? How can I explain my vote to those who elected me? Am I to tell them that I may have inadvertently voted in favour of a motion to concur in a Bill that would increase their taxes because I did not understand the motion? How can we prevent this situation from occurring if we are not clear on whether or not the Ways and Means motion will result in increased or decreased charges to our constituents?
In an attempt to help resolve this question in my own mind with respect to the motion in question, I consulted with the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon), and other staff members, about the wording of the motion. It has become clear that those five paragraphs, which you indicated earlier were unclear, become somewhat less confusing after referring to the free trade agreement. However, there still remains some doubt as to whether or not these paragraphs are relieving measures or will result in additional charges to the taxpayer. Therefore, I, as a Member of the House, am left with questions in my mind about the question I am being asked to decide upon. I think you would agree that this is a very confusing situation at the very least.
In recent years the Government has initiated Ways and Means motions, specifically those that arise out of budget legislation, which are detailed and specific. It is quite clear to the House just what we are being asked to vote upon. However, this five-paragraph motion tabled yesterday gives Members no such guidance whatsoever. It is totally incomplete.
I still maintain that if this motion is based upon the contents of the free trade agreement, it can contain no measures that increase the charge on taxpayers and thus is totally unnecessary as a preliminary step to the introduction of the free trade legislation. As such, and as I stated earlier, it limits the ability of Members of the House to amend the legislation that will eventually follow.
However, if you are of the opinion that these arguments are not convincing, then I submit, as I argued this morning, that the Ways and Means motion proposed by the Minister should be ruled out of order because it is, as you have stated yourself, unclear and therefore I as a Member of this House cannot be expected to decide on a question that is unclear.
I hope you will reflect on my arguments and perhaps return at a later time to make a ruling. I thank you for your patience in hearing my arguments at this moment.
Point of Order-Mr. Riis

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: NECESSITY OF WAYS AND MEANS MOTION
speechtext:
I have listened very carefully to the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) both yesterday and today. I indicated yesterday that whatever may be the final outcome, it seems to me that it was premature for the Chair to make a ruling. I have had time to reflect on the matter brought to my attention yesterday, and I have listened very carefully to the Hon. Member's complete argument again today. However, I remain of the same view. It is inappropriate for the Chair to try to make a ruling until the Chair sees what is actually in the proposed Bill. This does not mean that at that time it might not be appropriate to make a ruling.
I would add as a caveat that even if a ruling were made in accordance with the suggestion of the Hon. Member, it might not change anything very much. It might indicate that the Government had gone through an unnecessary process but it might not have any real substantive effect upon proceedings in the House.
I would ask the Hon. Member, who has raised a matter of importance, and certainly one of ingenuity, to accept the Chair's decision at this point that it would be premature to make an order. That does not mean I may not have further observations to make on the matter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: NECESSITY OF WAYS AND MEANS MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments are not intended to reflect in any way on what you just said, but I wish to raise with Your Honour the question of whether the Ways and Means motion is sufficiently complete in itself and sufficiently understandable that Members can make a decision upon it through their vote. There are problems with the motion in so far as it is not clear exactly what it is intended to do and say.
It is not enough for the Government to say it will introduce a Bill as a result of this motion being passed, if it is, and then everything will become clear. Surely it must be necessary for the Government, if it wishes to have a Ways and Means motion properly before the House, to have the content of the motion drafted so that it is clear to anyone voting upon it exactly what it intends to accomplish with respect to changes in the fiscal measures in question.
I respectfully submit that this is not the case and therefore the motion is defective and cannot be put before the House in its present form because Members are not in a position, from looking at the motion alone and not at a whole range of extraneous matters, to know just what they are voting upon.

subtopic: NECESSITY OF WAYS AND MEANS MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the point raised by the House Leader of the Official Opposition, I want to refer to Beau-chesne's Fifth Edition which says, in Citation 237, that a point of order against procedure must be raised promptly, which has been done, and before the question has passed to a stage at which the objection would be out of place. The point we are trying to make is that at some point in the future, if your ruling were that we ought to proceed, it might be out of place or beyond the point where such an intervention would be appropriate.

May 19, 1988
Ways and Means
Erskine May has perhaps indicated a way around this dilemma. At page 447 it says that doubtful cases may arise upon which the rules of the House are indistinct or obsolete or do not apply directly to the point at issue. I submit that such is the case at this point. It goes on to say that the Speaker will then usually give a ruling to cover the new circumstances, although he has on occasion referred the matter to the judgment of the House. Perhaps that would be the appropriate way to proceed now and simply refer this decision to the House itself.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: NECESSITY OF WAYS AND MEANS MOTION
speechtext:
I have listened very carefully to the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) and the further remarks of the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). While the points made by the Hon. Member for Windsor West were delivered with force, it seems to me they amount to essentially the same point raised by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap, and I remain of the view that it is premature for the Chair to rule.
The latter point that the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap makes I think can be met by the Chair making it very clear that I certainly do not think 1 am precluded from commenting on this at a later time. I think I have made it clear that if it is appropriate, I certainly will do so. I will not take the position, nor will 1 be persuaded to take the position, that I do not have a clear right as Speaker to consider the matter when I see the Bill.

Constitution Amendment, 1987

1. The Constitution Act, 1867 is amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 1 thereof, the following section:
"2. (1) The Constitution of Canada shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with
(a)	the recognition that the existence of French-speaking Canadians, centred in Quebec but also present elsewhere in Canada, and Englishspeaking Canadians, concentrated outside Quebec but also present in Quebec, constitutes a fundamental characteristic of Canada; and
(b)	the recognition that Quebec constitutes within Canada a distinct society.
(2)	The role of the Parliament of Canada and the provincial legislatures to preserve the fundamental characteristic of Canada referred to in paragraph (l)(a) is affirmed.
(3)	The role of the legislature and Government of Quebec to preserve and promote the distinct identity of Quebec referred to in paragraph (l)(b) is affirmed.
(4)	Nothing in this section derogates from the powers, rights or privileges of Parliament or the Government of Canada, or of the legislatures or governments of the provinces, including any powers, rights or privileges relating to language."
2.	The said Act is further amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 24 thereof, the following section:
"25. (1) Where a vacancy occurs in the Senate, the government of the province to which the vacancy relates may, in relation to that vacancy, submit to the Queen's Privy Council for Canada the names of persons who may be summoned to the Senate.
(2)	Until an amendment to the Constitution of Canada is made in relation to the Senate pursuant to section 41 of the Constitution Act, 1982, the person summoned to fill a vacancy in the Senate shall be chosen from among persons whose names have been submitted under subsection (1) by the government of the province to which the vacancy relates and must be acceptable to the Queen's Privy Council for Canada."
3.	The said Act is further amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 95 thereof, the following heading and sections:

95A. The Government of Canada shall, at the request of the government of any province, negotiate with the government of that province for the purpose of concluding an agreement relating to immigration or the temporary admission of aliens into that province that is appropriate to the needs and circumstances of that province.
95B. (1) Any agreement concluded between Canada and a province in relation to immigration or the temporary admission of aliens into that province has the force of law from the time it is declared to do so in accordance with subsection 95C(1) and shall from that time have effect notwithstanding class 25 of section 91 or section 95.
(2)	An agreement that has the force of law under subsection (1) shall have effect only so long and so far as it is not repugnant to any provision of an Act of the Parliament of Canada that sets national standards and objectives relating to immigration or aliens, including any provision that establishes general classes of immigrants or relates to levels of immigration for Canada or that prescribes classes of individuals who are inadmissible into Canada.
(3)	The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms applies in respect of any agreement that has the force of law under subsection (1) and in respect of anything done by the Parliament or Government of Canada, or the legislature or government of a province, pursuant to any such agreement.
95C. (1) A declaration that an agreement referred to in subsection 95B(1) has the force of law may be made by proclamation issued by the Governor General under the Great Seal of Canada only where so authorized by resolutions of the Senate and House of Commons and of the legislative assembly of the province that is a party to the agreement.
(2) An amendment to an agreement referred to in subsection 95B(1) may be made by proclamation issued by the Governor General under the Great Seal of Canada only where so authorized
(a)	by resolutions of the Senate and House of Commons and of the
legislative assembly of the province that is a party to the agreement; or
(b)	in such other manner as is set out in the agreement.

subsubtopic: DESTRUCTION OF TROPICAL FORESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the World Resource Institute reports that many developing countries have lost billions of dollars through timber subsidies and giveaways that accelerate destruction of tropical forests. Developing countries are collecting royalties and taxes just a fraction of what the timber is worth. The result of such policies is the extensive, wasteful, rapid destruction of resources.
The United Nations estimates that about 27 million acres of forests are being lost in developing countries each year. In addition, the World Resources Institute points out that the under-valuing and over-harvesting of timber are our problem as well. The estimate is in the hundreds of millions of dollars a year lost in the United States.
In Canada we suffer from the same problems. We have low royalties and extensive, wasteful, rapid destruction of our
May 19, 1988

forests. I ask the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merri-thew) to examine this problem urgently. Our forests should be managed in a sustainable manner.

Mr. Speaker, this is National Tourism Awareness Week. It is a time to praise the work of those people who work in the tourism industry. Tourism is our nation's fifth largest industry. It may well become Canada's second largest industrialized sector by the year 2000.
By the end of last year tourism was Canada's third largest earner of foreign exchange. It is labour intensive, offering work to 600,000 Canadians. More jobs are created indirectly by tourism expenditures. Tourism is important, too, for regional development, stimulating economic growth in the less industrialized regions of Canada.
The level of tourism today is double what it was 10 years ago. Statistics Canada reports that during the first 11 months of 1987, international travel to Canada surpassed all records. The reasons for this are quite obvious. Canada has become a world-class destination, second to none for international travellers.

subtopic: REFUGEE STATUS ADVISORY COMMITTEE-REVERSAL OF DECISION
REFUGEE STATUS ADVISORY COMMITTEE-REVERSAL OF DECISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall), at the behest of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), is frustrating the clear intent of the Immigration Act and bringing the law into disrespect among the public and the legal community.
The Minister rejected the lawfully made recommendation of highly qualified members of the Refugee Status Advisory Committee, and, in effect, fired them for doing their job according to law. She then accepted the opinion of bureaucrats who lack qualification, authority or experience in determining refugee status.
She has in fact attempted to apply part of Bill C-55 while it has not been passed by Parliament-that is, she is using a vague and unproven security accusation to deny Mr. Santokh Singh his lawful right to an unbiased hearing.
Accordingly, she has provoked a boycott of the Refugee Status Advisory Committee by the National Chairman and
other leading members of the immigration section of the Canadian Bar Association.
I call on the Minister to reverse her unjust and scoff-law decision, or else resign.

Mr. Speaker, a story on the front page of yesterday's Montreal Gazette indicates why crime remains rampant in Canada and will be soothing to the bleeding hearts who think more of the criminals than they do of the victims. A sadistic 32-year-old habitual criminal who raped women at gunpoint was convicted on 22 offences which included forceful confinement, weapon use, theft, sexual assault, and crimes of physical violence. Some of the women may never be the same again.
"These crimes pollute the community," the judge said, and sentenced the criminal, who has already served 19 years behind bars, to a total of 123 years in prison. Do you know what, Mr. Speaker? Under our present system this criminal will be eligible for parole in seven years. Why should a person with a record like this ever again be released into society?

Mr. Speaker, when the Conservative Government said it would participate in the space station that is part of the U.S. government's space program, the Minister of Industry and Trade announced that the economic spin-offs and jobs would be shared equally between Quebec and Ontario, in other words, 35 per cent each.
Furthermore, for months and even for the last two years, the Conservative Government has given the impression and led the people of Montreal to believe that the space agency would be located in Montreal. This morning we read that the National Research Centre has already awarded contracts, including the most important ones, for space research. Unfortunately, contrary to the promise that was made, Quebec has received only 26 per cent. Mr. Speaker, this is one more instance where the Conservative Government has failed to keep its promises to Quebecers.

subtopic: ETABLISHMENT OF NEW CLUB IN DUBERGER
ETABLISHMENT OF NEW CLUB IN DUBERGER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure and pride that I take this opportunity to draw the attention of the House today to an event that is very important to the people of Duberger, and I am referring to the creation of a new Optimist Club.
Mr. Speaker, this service club, which is mainly involved in youth programs and has a reputation for generous and effective community involvement, is a valuable addition to any community and enjoys the regard and respect of those they have helped through their activities.
The optimist philosophy transcends race, colour, creed and class. With an optimistic outlook, a person, group or even a nation can accomplish the impossible. Without optimism, the battle is lost before the first shot is fired. On April 30, the Optimists of Duberger officially took their first step towards a formidable goal.
I want to congratulate Mr. Claude Forest, the first president of the Optimist Club of Duberger, and all those who made this project possible. I wish them every success in their work with our youth!

Mr. Speaker, the resolve of the people of western Canada is being tested again. A devastating drought continues to turn fertile, productive farmland into parched, barren fields.
Scenes reminiscent of the early 1930s have filled our television screens, alerting all Canadians to the sorry plight of many farmers forced to abandon a way of life because of a cruel quirk of fate.
In stark contrast, the premiers of the four western provinces are now meeting in regal splendour to discuss this latest crisis. They are holding their talks on a private $3 million luxury liner. They will be ferried to and from their pleasure boat by a fleet of gleaming white stretch limousines, each one customized with personalized licence plates.
Their extravagance is galling. It reflects the shameful insensitivity of western Canadian Premiers to the difficulties facing western Canadian citizens.

subtopic: INVITATION TO DRUMMONDVILLE WORLD FOLKLORE FESTIVAL
INVITATION TO DRUMMONDVILLE WORLD FOLKLORE FESTIVAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to invite all Members and all Canadians to the riding of Drummond, where the Seventh World Folklore Festival will be held from July 8 to 18.

Each year, in early July, the Drummondville World Folklore Festival welcomes entertainers from more than 15 countries, with 40 exceptionally talented folklore groups and more than 1,500 musicians, singers, and dancers offering over 300 shows. Last year more than 700,000 spectators attended the festival's various events.

The World Folklore Festival welcomes you to its many activities, to a magic rendez-vous where masks will be the theme of the festivities.
Enjoy this world of folklore where day and night, dancing, music, shows, concerts, special programs and parades will be a feast for the eyes, ears and heart.
Don't miss the World Folklore Festival in Drummondville!

CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF CONSUMERS OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to the National Association of Consumers of Quebec, the free trade agreement is a lemon. Marie Vezina, the spokesperson for this group, told La Presse that they had used statistics and trade numbers from the Department of Finance as a basis for their research. They came to the conclusion that the Mulroney trade deal is bad for Canada, especially with respect to electricity, hydro, tariffs and telephone services.
Marie Vezina is encouraging all members of that organization to oppose the agreement during the upcoming election.

A GRANDMOTHER'S GIFT-BANK'S LESSON FOR ONE-YEAR OLD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday it came to my attention that one of Canada's largest banks set a world record for levying a deterrent charge on its youngest customer.
Jake Mastandrea had to be taught a lesson on his first birthday. His grandmother wrote him a cheque for $25 as his birthday present. Although the cheque indicated $25 she inadvertently left off the five in recording the amount. The cheque was returned and Jake was assessed a penalty of $5 for depositing his grandmother's birthday gift. Incidentally, his grandmother, who deals with National Trust, was not assessed a penalty because they do not charge for simple customer errors.
When I was a little boy my mother used to recite one of Little Orphan Annie's poems ending with the warning "The goblins will get you if you don't watch out". Perhaps today's mothers should be warning their children that "The banker-man will get you if you don't watch out".

Mr. Speaker, there are about
232.000	households currently served by supermailboxes. About
175.000	are serviced by contractors at an annual cost of $35, and the balance serviced by post office letter carriers at a cost of $97. Full delivery by letter carriers costs $120 per household. Going door-to-door for all existing supermailboxes would therefore cost about $16 million a year.
Canada Post projects another 500,000 supermailboxes will be added over the next three years. About half will be the result of lower cost supermailboxes in new subdivisions. Extending door-to-door delivery to them all would cost an extra $86 per address, or about $22 million. Add that to the $16 million, and the total additional cost is $38 million.
A one cent increase in the price of mailing a letter generates $25 million, so it would cost less than two cents to axe the supermailbox program.
I say that two cents is a small price to pay for equality and fairness. Let us hope the Minister pays a bigger price in the next election for not understanding that.

Mr. Speaker, dioxins and furans are deadly toxic substances found in pulp and paper effluents and in shellfish and molluscs in then vicinity.
The reaction of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. MacMillan), the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) to studies about this problem shows a shocking complacency. They say that not all of the samples showed high levels of dioxin or furans. They say there are some excuses that can be found in the cases where there are high levels. "A small amount of dioxin is fine for one's health, but just do not have
second helpings". "Dioxins in the organ parts of an animal are a problem, so avoid that part of the body". "Chicken livers are contaminated, well, eat the wings". This is bad policy in principle, apart from the fact that some people do eat the organ parts of shellfish and consider them a delicacy.
Another statement made in the report was that excess dioxins were found in areas close to mollusc fishing in any event, so let us not worry about it. These are deadly substances. It is a serious problem. It is a crisis. This kind of complacency is shockingly irresponsible. I call upon the Government to take the problem seriously and clean up this highly contaminated substance.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last time I rose in the House of Commons to speak in favour of the Meech Lake Accord, we had just received the report of the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on the 1987 constitutional Accord. Members will recall the enormous efforts made by the joint committee last summer to hear and assess the views of interested Canadians.
During the course of their deliberations, the committee gave extremely close attention to divergent views regarding major elements of the Accord, and provided us with a thorough and compelling report. The committee recommended the adoption of the 1987 constitutional Accord, which this House adopted by resolution on October 26, 1987.
The other place has since considered the resolution, and the 180-day period during which a constitutional amendment is not possible without the authorization of the other place has expired.
Four provincial and legislative assemblies have now adopted the Accord and others are holding hearings. In short, the amending process set out in the Constitution Act, 1982, is being followed.
The last time that I spoke with respect to this motion I attempted to put the Accord into perspective. While it is certainly a tremendous achievement, restoring the Province of Quebec to its rightful place as an equal participant in the Canadian constitutional family, it is also the mark of an important beginning for our country from which we can move ahead, united, to address issues of mutual concern.
The Accord deals with the most urgent constitutional matters that face us today in the context of national reconciliation. Bearing this in mind, there are two points which I stated on that previous occasion and which merit emphasis again today. First, despite considerable rhetoric on various points, no egregious errors have been shown to exist in the Accord. Second, to re-open the Accord on any other basis would be contrary to the commitment of First Ministers and would inevitably destroy the chances for future constitutional reform.
Therefore, I would ask Members to consider the consequences of failure after having come this far. Consider the consequences of the rest of Canada saying no to Quebec a second time, after Quebec was left isolated and humiliated in 1981.
Since 1982, constitutional reform has been blocked. Four conferences on aboriginal rights ended in failure, partly because Quebec declined to participate actively at First Ministers conferences.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
As Professor Peter Meekison, former Deputy Minister of Federal and Intergovernmental affairs in Alberta and one of Canada's leading constitutional practitioners, testified before the joint committee:
I think the consequences of Quebec's not accepting this are incalculable ...
Given the importance that Alberta places on Senate reform, there will not be
debate on Senate reform until Quebec is in the Constitution.
He went on to say:
Get this behind us, then everything else can be discussed.
I think it is important to review what was accomplished in the Meech Lake Accord. Meech Lake was never expected to be a cure for the myriad problems and challenges facing our nation. Rather, it was a vital First step in meeting our commitment to the people of Quebec and ensuring that they were an equal partner in the future growth of our nation.
There are clearly many other issues of concern which could have been addressed and which will need to be considered in future rounds. But the test of this resolution is whether it meets the basic objective which was set forward by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the 10 provincial Premiers, namely to obtain Quebec's willing adherence to the Canadian Constitution. I submit that it does.
Once adopted, future generations of Canadians and their leaders will never have to face the consequence of Quebec's continued estrangement from our constitutional development.
It has been alleged by some that the Charter is being weakened, the rights of linguistic minorities and the equality rights of women are somehow threatened. I can say unequivocally that this is false.
Professor Peter Hogg, one of Canada's foremost constitutional experts, writes that the Charter of Rights is clearly paramount over a distinct society clause. He writes:
A law passed to preserve linguistic duality or to promote the distinct identity
of Quebec would, like any other law, have to comply with the Charter.
The Charter will, in future, be interpreted in light of Quebec's distinctiveness as it now is in light of multicultural and aboriginal heritage considerations.
When we say that Quebec constitutes a distinct society within Canada, it is understood that all residents of Quebec are an integral part of that society. Thus, Quebec's aboriginal population is part of that distinct society within Canada. Those Quebecers from a multicultural community are part of it, Quebec's English speaking community is an integral part of Quebec's distinct society. All Quebecers belong to that distinct society, which enriches the diversity of Canada.
One has to wonder why this Accord, with its laudable goals, is before us again today. As Hon. Members are aware, the constitutional amendment process was initiated by the Quebec National Assembly on June 23, 1987. On October 26, 1987, by an overwhelming majority of 242 to 16 votes, and with the support of all three Party Leaders, this House approved the Meech Lake Accord as embodied in our resolution. Prior to

May 19, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
the adoption of the resolution, on September 23, 1987, the Legislative Assembly of my own home Province of Saskatchewan adopted the Accord by a vote of 43 to 3. Subsequently, on December 7, 1987, the Legislative Assembly of Alberta adopted the Accord by a unanimous vote.
The Accord was tabled in Ontario on November 5, 1987, and referred to a select committee on November 30. On February 26, 1988, the Accord was tabled in the Legislative Assembly of Nova Scotia. It was tabled in the Legislative Assembly of Newfoundland on March 25, 1988. It was tabled in the Legislative Assembly of Prince Edward Island on March 29, 1988, and adopted on May 13 of this year. From these events, it is evident that Canadians across the land have joined in the process of welcoming the national reconciliation embodied in the Accord.
Some of the appointed Members in the other place, after consideration of the resolution, have not seen fit to adopt it in the form authorized by the House of Commons. The actions of some Members of the Senate remind me, and probably many other Members of Parliament and many other Canadians, of just how out of touch some Members of that body have become with respect to the views and aspirations of Canadians. I regret very much that this movement in the other place was undertaken by the Liberal majority whose own Leader has stood here and spoken unequivocally in favour of this resolution. Those Liberal Senators have seen fit to go against the wishes of their Leader. They have undertaken a very careful plan to undermine this particular constitutional amendment.
Most witnesses in the other place received the courtesy of attention, but I do not think I have seen a more curious sight than the former Prime Minister of our country, the Right Hon. Pierre Trudeau, who was accorded between six and seven hours to stand before those whom he appointed to that place and lecture them with respect to this Accord. The irony of that is simply that each and every principle contained in this constitutional Accord was accepted at one time or other by the Right Hon. Pierre Trudeau when he was Prime Minister.
That is false.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a fact. It has been documented. I ask what the point is in coming back before Senators he appointed and attempting to undermine a very important constitutional movement? I say with a sense of sadness, and without any partisanship, that the Liberal Party of Canada has had a proud tradition of being sensitive with respect to the aspirations of the Province of Quebec. I give full credit to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) for the leadership he has given in supporting this constitutional amendment because it is important to the Province of Quebec and it is fundamental to this country. I do not make any apologies for supporting that position and putting it forward to the Liberal Senators.
You don't have to attack the former Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am sorry. He has come forward and attempted to undermine this very important initiatives. I am not attacking him personally. He is entitled, as any other person in this country, to his opinion. But I simply reiterate the fact that I found it incredibly ironic that former Prime Minister Trudeau would attack principles which he himself had embraced in his attempt to bring about constitutional amendments in this country. I state that as the reality of what we face today. I do not understand the purpose of this attack on his part.
Those in the other place who form a majority have single-handedly attempted to rewrite history and amend an agreement which has received the approval of 10 provinces and, as I indicated, of three Party Leaders, and an overwhelming vote in favour of that by the House of Commons. These are people who are elected and accountable. They have to go back to the people of Canada and defend the positions they have taken here. We have a responsibility and sensitivity to this issue which I think should not be overlooked by the other place.
A joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons looked at this matter in some detail. The report is there. Four provincial legislative assemblies have already passed this particular constitutional amendment. I can only refer, I think, with approval, to the words of my colleague in the other place, the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Senator Murray) the Leader of the Government in the Senate, who stated during the course of debate:
The amendments proposed by the Opposition would require the Governments to reopen practically all the sections of an agreement that has unanimous support.
I suggest that those who propose such amendments are not seeking to improve the Accord, as they claim. The amendments being proposed are killer amendments. They have only one purpose in mind-they are designed to kill the Accord.
I urge Hon. Members opposite not to propose amendments. Such proposals could only encourage their provincial cousins to seek to reopen the Accord for renegotiation. Rather than proposing amendments that would risk the unanimity achieved by First Ministers, this House and provincial legislatures should rejoice in the achievement of the Accord and hasten to demonstrate our collective responsibility for national unity, and the generosity of spirit which has marked our history, by adopting the resolution without further delay.
Fortunately, the Members appointed to the other place do not have the power to override the collective will of the democratically elected representatives of the people in their provincial and federal legislative assemblies. Canadians have an obligation to ensure that the popular national will on a matter of the most fundamental importance to our country is not stifled by unelected opposition Members in the other place. In fact, the Constitution expressly provides that an amendment may be made without a resolution of the Senate if the House of Commons again adopts the resolution after the expiration of
May 19, 1988

the 180 days from the time the House of Commons first adopted the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, when this House again passes the resolution, we will not only overturn the temporary veto of the other place, but we will also send a message of encouragement and support to all those who believe in the spirit and the letter of the Meech Lake Accord. We will honour the commitment of the Government of Canada to underscore officially Quebec's return to the Canadian family.
Mr. Speaker, Quebec has said yes to Canada. A vote for the Meech Lake Accord will be important evidence of our commitment to Quebec and to building harmonious relations for our country's future.

In 1982, in the aftermath of the Quebec referendum of 1980, with the concurrence of nine provinces, with the concurrence of this House, with the concurrence of the other place, with the concurrence of the Parliament of the United Kingdom and with the approval of the Supreme Court of Canada, we in this country adopted the Constitution Act, 1982. Unfortunately, at that time, the Province of Quebec was isolated by this process. Its feeling of alienation has been a cause of great concern and grave concern ever since.
The Province of Quebec subsequently opted out of the application of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to the greatest extent possible because it had not approved it. In addition, the absence of Quebec effectively prevented possible constitutional amendments of great importance pursuant to the new amending formula. Quebec refused to participate in any such amendments because it would be implemented pursuant to the Constitution Act, 1982, to which Quebec had not given its assent.
These have been some of the most visible past consequences of Quebec's isolation in 1982. The people of Canada, through their elected representatives, have dedicated themselves to solving the problem of Quebec's isolation as a matter of national priority. If we are to avoid the grave consequences of failure, we must not be side-tracked either by unmerited criticisms or by worthy issues whose time for consideration or reconsideration has yet to come.
Our first constitutional amendment today must be to complete the Quebec round of our constitutional reforms. Only then will we have secured the complete legitimacy of our full constitutional framework, and only then will we be able to build successfully on our past accomplishments. The present moment must belong to Quebec so that the future may belong to all Canadians.

We are all very aware that many important points must still be dealt with under constitutional reform. The Meech Lake
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Accord is a basis for moving forward on the protection of minority language rights, Senate reform, the rights of native people and all other issues. If it were only up to the Senate, we would be condemned to dwell in the past. Mr. Speaker, if we cannot consolidate our constitutional gains, we are in danger of spending decades on a costly, futile, divisive constitutional debate. Is this what the other House wants?

Worse still, as Premier Peterson said on April 28:
If this opportunity is missed, my own political assessment is that you won't see that opportunity again.
He concluded that the judgment of history would be very harsh.
These sentiments were reflected in the comments of the Hon. J. W. Pickersgill, who held a number of important public offices under four Prime Ministers, when he told the joint committee in no uncertain terms:
If Quebec is rebuffed, if this Accord becomes discord, and the opportunity is lost to get acquiescence of the constitutional authorities in Quebec, my guess is that it probably will not arise again for another generation, and never again on such reasonable terms.
What I want is for the patriotic sentiment and generous spirit that characterized this round of constitutional reform to become the rule and not the exception so that future progress may also be realized.
We cannot afford to lose this precedent of goodwill, reasonableness and common sense leading to constitutional reform pursuant to the most rigid of our constitutional amending formulae. We have before us an Accord that has been endorsed with pride and enthusiasm, an Accord that unifies and strengthens Canada. To reopen this Accord would be to lose it.
What possible justification can there be to postpone national reconciliation to a time when the chances of success may be far less and the most severe consequences of failure more immediate?
Has an egregious error been found? No, Mr. Speaker. Have First Ministers failed to consider all the issues placed before them? No, Mr. Speaker. Does unanimous agreement exist to reopen the Accord for renegotiation? No, Mr. Speaker.
It comes down to one question. Should Canada say no to Quebec? For that would surely be the effect of reopening the Accord without a legitimate reason for doing so. There is no reason for this. It is time for us as Canadians, as Members of Parliament, to say yes to Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, the 1987 constitutional amendment is not the end of the constitutional reform process. A thorough examination of constitutional questions will remain an important element of our search for the most appropriate solutions to the fundamental problems that we as a nation must face. I hope that when it comes to consider these matters, the other

May 19, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Chamber will finally see the significance of our decision to pass this resolution again.

Mr. Speaker, 130 years ago a great man of another great nation quoted to his country the biblical warning that a house divided against itself cannot stand. The wisdom of such common sense should appeal to us.
Canada's history is somewhat unique in the way we have continually created harmony out of seemingly discordant national elements. This is the glory of our past and the strength of our future. The Constitution Amendment, 1987 continues this tradition. It envisions a nation moving ever closer to a more co-operative and tolerant way of life and of government. It is a vision in which we can take pride.
The Meech Lake Accord deserves our enthusiastic support. I invite Hon. Members to reaffirm our commitment to the resolution by adopting it once again.
There is a momentum, a desire on the part of Canadians to move forward to seek the ratification of this Accord which I commend to Hon. Members.
What about the Gallup poll?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not want to trivialize this debate or the considerations with respect to this matter by entering into any type of regime in which Gallup polls or, indeed, whatever polls are taken from time to time are brought forward. I can only say that it is unusual in the history of our country to have a situation in which we have unanimity among the First Ministers of the provinces and of the federal Government, as well as of all the Leaders in the House of Commons. It is not giving me any satisfaction that we cannot get unanimity across the whole country. But that is impossible.
I think that the people who have the greatest stake in this on behalf of the people of Canada are those who have to face the electorate, those people who have to be re-elected to justify the positions that they take. They have made a decision. This is quite apart from Party and partisan politics. Members from every political Party represented in this House have in fact approved this Accord.
This is an opportunity for those who feel that they want to block this to consider the consequences of what they do. If they want by their actions to return to the situation in which we will again isolate the Province of Quebec, then I think that they will have to stand accountable for the positions they take. I do not have the privilege of coming from the Province of Quebec. However, I come from another part of our country, the Province of Saskatchewan.
That is a privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is a western province which has very happily accepted this amendment in overwhelming numbers and with overwhelming support.
Distinct society?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is something that binds us together. I do not regard this as being an accord which, in fact, does anything but strengthen this nation. For the benefit of Members, I explained that to me a distinct society in Quebec is a very understandable and important consideration which does not in any way diminish the Charter of Rights and the rights of minorities. The Province of Quebec today consists of a great variety of minorities and a very important number of aboriginal peoples. All of them together, with the French majority and the English minority, do constitute a unique society.
I simply say to Hon. Members, who are determined to oppose this, that I hope they will give consideration to the consequences of their actions. As the years go by after this is passed and they see how it has strengthened our country and brought a unity and co-operation together, they will be able to say, contrary to their present position today, that this was one of the finest moments in the history of the House of Commons of Canada.
