Mr. Speaker, I have concluded the specific points I wanted to refer to in the Meech Lake Accord. I have explained our amendments and indicated why we find the Meech Lake Accord a positive step forward and why we intend to support it. The Minister of Justice when he stood up to introduce this order of business was very critical of the Senate. I do not think his criticism was justified.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
I think the Senate has done nothing more in the process than to demonstrate what ought to be done with the amendments that have been brought forward by the Official Opposition, how compatible they are with the Meech Lake Accord, and how they take nothing away from the constitutional priorities of the Province of Quebec. Surely, it also demonstrates how other matters could be added, matters including multicultural-ism, the strengthening of the economic union of Canada, the establishment of a proper voice throughout the entire Meech Lake Accord for the northern people of Canada who were sidelined by the Meech Lake Accord, hopefully through an oversight, but one which could easily be corrected and which the Senate did correct. I regret that no effort has been made to amend the Meech Lake Accord and to see if that can be done within the context of an agreement so that this important constitutional step which is a positive step can be taken.
In conclusion, I think that the Government has made a terrible mistake in tactics in insisting that the Meech Lake Accord is a seamless web, that it is perfect and that only egregious error would justify reopening it. If surveys tell us anything, the Government ought to recognize that Canadians would like to see some of the important points the Official Opposition has made adopted in the Meech Lake Accord.
Finally, I want to assure the Government that our support is firm. We want this constitutional step forward to take place, but an examination of the state of support across Canada might indicate that its adoption or constitutionalization could be greatly enhanced by the consideration and acceptance of the amendments which have been put forward by the Official Opposition.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party, I would like to begin by saying how very appreciative we are that the Meech Lake Accord should return to the House. We are not particularly appreciative of what the Senate tried to do with the Accord, but the other place has given us the opportunity once again to discuss the Accord, and for that we are very grateful.
I say that because in the view of Members of this Party, Meech Lake and what has been said about Meech Lake over the past several months has reinforced rather than diminished our support for the Accord. It has reinforced in several important respects our belief that Meech Lake is actually stronger and more effective than we had even dreamed at the time that it would be.
Let me start by giving a few illustrations of the fact that in our view, Meech Lake is stronger, better and more effective than we ever dreamed it could be. The first illustration concerns what happened with the introduction of Bill 2 in the Saskatchewan Legislature, effectively limiting the long established legal rights of the Francophone linguistic minority in that province. If Meech Lake were already in effect, it is our

May 19, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
firm belief that that limiting action of the Saskatchewan Government would have been declared contrary to the Constitution as amended by Meech Lake.
I know that it might sound incredibly machiavellian to suggest that a Premier would want to limit francophone rights so that when Meech Lake kicked in, he would have fewer rights to preserve. However, I honestly believe that despite the fact that the Premier signed the agreement and despite the fact that the legislature passed it by a 43 to 3 vote, he circumvented it. He said to himself: "If I wait until the provisions of the Constitutional Accord are formally adopted, I will find that it is the duty of this province to preserve the legal rights of the francophone minority, including the right for the translation of laws into French". This is because Meech Lake, as we have been reminded many times, requires provincial legislatures to preserve the official linguistic minorities of Canada.
I recall that on the committee, there was some discussion about whether the Accord should not both preserve and promote linguistic duality. Many of us thought that that would be desirable, but then we realized that to have all the provinces of Canada, and particularly, I may say, the western provinces, agree to preserve linguistic duality would indeed be a very major step ahead. We assumed that the provinces would be preserving everything from French on cornflakes boxes in British Columbia to the legal language rights of the Francophones of Saskatchewan.
With this rather transparent attempt to restrict the rights to be preserved, we have been shown vividly the importance of the clause in Meech Lake requiring the preservation of existing minority language rights.
As a second illustration, we have also realized over the last several months that many of the naysayers on Meech Lake, including the former Prime Minister, Pierre Elliott Trudeau, are effectively saying that two linguistic Canadas are being created by Meech Lake, French in Quebec, English everywhere else. Time and time again in the past several months, we have heard this. It would seem to me that those who keep saying this have simply not read the new Section 2 of the Constitution embodied in this Accord. Above all, they have not read that the duties of the provincial legislatures to preserve linguistic duality are duties that are shared and must be shared just as much by the legislature of Quebec as by any other legislature.
The two Canadas, one French and the rest English, seems to me to imply that there would be no provision in Meech Lake requiring the legislature of Quebec, as it does of all other legislatures, to preserve linguistic duality. I think that a very large disservice has been done to the very goal the former Prime Minister wanted to achieve; namely, an officially bilingual Canada, when even he suggests that Meech Lake is destroying that goal and that vision. It does a very, very serious disservice to the Accord.
I noticed just the other day that in the National Assembly of Quebec, specifically April 29, the Minister responsible for languages, Guy Rivard, made it absolutely clear, if there had ever been any doubt in the mind of Mr. Trudeau or anyone else, that Quebec's large 200-year old anglophone community is "an integral part of the character of our distinct society". So the succession of fears aroused in the last several months, that somehow the Accord is going to divide us into a French Quebec and an English everything else are simply not justified and must be dissipated.
A third development over the last several months which has shown the strength of Meech Lake is in the area of federal spending power. We have had a succession of journalists, I am sorry to say, and politicians, I am even sorrier to say, suggesting over the past several months that under the new constitutional Accord it will no longer be possible to have national social programs. Just today I read a CP story in The Toronto Star which said that the Accord would "limit the right of the federal Government to introduce new national shared-cost programs like medicare". This is simply not true. This just instils fear in the minds of people, particularly the disadvantaged and disabled in our society, that we will never again be able to have national shared-cost programs like medicare. Of course, if that were true, we would be justified in being fearful. I would be fearful, too.
I have talked to large numbers of people in the Coalition for the Disabled, visible minorities, and many others, who say that they have now been convinced there is no longer going to be any kind of social program possible for them in the future. The naysayers and scaremongers who are saying these things apparently do not yet grasp the fact that for the first time it is now written in the Constitution of Canada that there can be national shared-cost programs in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction. That has never ever been in the Constitution of Canada. Ever since Borden, federal Governments have engaged in spending in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction in developing shared-cost programs, but it has never been constitutionalized. So, far from retreating from the possibility of having national shared-cost programs, and I am thinking primarily of social programs but there would be economic programs as well, the Accord strengthens and constitutionalizes the possibility of future programs.
I am sorry to say that Mr. Trudeau has also added to the fears. He, who never launched a national social program in 16 years, who helped unravel several of the programs we did have, particularly that of post-secondary education, has the gall to suggest that we could not have national social programs under Meech Lake. It is just incredible gall.
Now you're talking.

That is what he has been suggesting while fanning the flames of fear.
May 19, 1988

I remind everyone in the Chamber that it was in the 1960s that we got our national social programs in key areas like medicare and the Canada Pension Plan during what we called an era of co-operative federalism. That is the kind of federalism that Meech Lake itself embraces. We did not get those national programs through dictation or usurpation of power. We got them through discussions between the federal and provincial authorities. In the case of medicare, it started when only two provinces were in agreement and then others came on board.
That was the era of the development of national social programs, and I am sorry to say that after the 1960s not only did we not have any more national social programs, but we found under the Established Programs Financing Act the federal Government relinquishing any authority over the spending of federal moneys, particularly in the area of postsecondary education.
That simply would not be possible under the Accord we are discussing once again today. A program in an area of exclusive provincial jurisdiction, initiated by the federal Government of Canada, and several provinces will undoubtedly have been talked to about it and will have indicated they are interested in participating in it, will only develop as the provinces themselves agree to spend the money for a program compatible with the national objectives of the program. In other words, national objectives have never been in our Constitution before. People talk about Balkanizing Canada. It is the contrary that is becoming increasingly evident over recent months.
National objectives can be just what you want them to be. They can be as tight as you want to make them. If the federal Government has the political will to do so, if you had a federal Government that really wanted accessible and universal child care on a non-profit basis, and unfortunately the present Government does not have that particular will, and you established those national objectives under the shared-cost program arrangement, it would be pretty difficult for any province that joined in to then spend that money on roads and bridges. That is what they have frequently done in the field of post-secondary education because Mr. Trudeau did not have any national vision on that matter. It would be very difficult indeed.
Just as I spoke a moment ago about the Province of Saskatchewan possibly trying to limit the French language rights that it would need to preserve before Meech Lake kicked in, so I think the federal Government itself has limited what it will do on child care and refused to define national objectives because it knew once Meech Lake became effective it would have to define national objectives. Even the federal Government is somewhat guilty of trying to implement certain policies before the strength of Meech Lake is finally put into the Constitution.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Another area which has been much discussed by the naysayers is what Meech Lake does to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The criticism is not only extreme, it is wrong. I read in the press that the Charter is practically being destroyed as a result of Meech Lake, that the Constitutional Accord alters the basic rights and powers spelled out in the Charter, and that the distinct society rule of interpretation will remove from Charter review any action by the Quebec Government or any other government under the linguistic duality rule.
There is a misperception that actions taken under the Accord either to preserve linguistic duality or promote the distinct identity of Quebec will be immune from Charter review. There is a misperception that they can freely infringe upon the Charter, which is simply not the case.
The final report of the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons last September pointed out that by virtue of Section 52 of the Constitution Act, 1982, any law, federal or provincial, or governmental Act that is inconsistent with the Constitution, including the Charter, is to the extent of the inconsistency, of no force or effect. What could be clearer?
Unless a new set of constitutional principles evolve in the future which none of us can even imagine, legislation or governmental action taken in furtherance of linguistic duality or the distinct society would be subject to Charter review according to normal constitutional principles.
We know that the rights in the Charter are not absolute and are, themselves, subject to Section 1 of the Charter, the reasonable rights section. A legislature must prove that any reasonable limit it wishes to apply to any particular right or freedom, including equality and non discrimination rights, can be demonstrably justified. That same proof would have to be provided if a legislature pursued a policy attempting to preserve linguistic duality which might limit one of the freedoms in the Charter. The onus of proof is on the legislature.
The same Charter review that applies now to all legislative Acts will apply to additional rules of interpretation relating to the distinct society and linguistic duality clauses. I suggest it is mischievous for commentators to continue saying that the Charter can be abrogated by the Meech Lake Accord.
The First Ministers contributed to the problem somewhat by removing two sections from the Charter and inserting them in Clause 16 of the Accord. This suggested that other parts of the Charter were not as important, but the explanation given for the inclusion of Sections 25 and 27 was that they were interpretative clauses relating to cultural matters.
Since the Accord primarily relates to linguistic and cultural matters, it was argued that it was important to include them but their interpretation would not affect the multicultural heritage of Canada or the rights of aboriginal peoples of Canada. I can sympathize with the concern of women and

May 19, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
minorities that the inclusion of those two sections somehow minimized their rights. That is why one of our amendments recommends that at least Section 28 of the Charter dealing with equality rights of men and women should be added to Clause 16 of the Accord.
The key section of the Charter, Section 15 dealing with non discrimination on the basis of race or sex, and Section 15(2) providing for affirmative action for disadvantaged groups, remain intact and will continue to exist without any effect from the Meech Lake Accord. Therefore, I hope we will not have to continue listening to what I must unfortunately call fear mongering. None of us want to receive letters from groups in our society about whom we are concerned, saying that they have been told that their rights will be abridged as a result of the Meech Lake Accord. That is simply not true.
In addition to our amendment to include Section 28 in Clause 16 of the Accord, we have also suggested other modest amendments about which my colleagues will expand. They relate to the unfair treatment of the Yukon and Northwest Territories by providing for unanimity in order to bring them into the nation, which is a far higher degree of consensus than has ever been required for other provinces.
We also want them to be able to make appointments for Supreme Court judges. We are very concerned about the absence of any provision in the Accord for the resumption of conferences on aboriginal rights, particularly native self government. The Native Council of Canada only recently published copies of its proposed draft companion amendments. All of them are included in our amendments that we proposed to the First Ministers. The first draft companion amendment is the reinstatement of the aboriginal reform process. The second concerns territorial representation in the Supreme Court, and a third is the establishment of provinces in the territories.
The Native Council of Canada also hoped to present a companion amendment relating to women, but I have not had seen that yet. In any event, they stated in their press release that the New Democratic Party has not taken seriously their proposal for companion amendments. On the contrary, the very content of its companion amendments is what we have already put in our amendments. The Council may say, and I think it does say in its press release, that the companion amendment approach is not anyone's first preference, that it would rather have the Accord amended. I can only agree with the Council. We want to have the Accord amended directly as well.
Our amendments, at least in the areas I have just been discussing, are similar to its companion amendments. There may be some later time down the road, but at the moment we in the New Democratic Party are still arguing that the small package of amendments we proposed before and are proposing again in no way gut the Accord. In no way do they deny the fundamental principles, but they do produce a degree of
fairness for northern people, native people and for women, that is not now present in the Accord.
We are still working to get our amendments adopted. There are two new premiers since we last spoke in this House and we are hoping that perhaps, with their understanding, we will be able to get our amendments back to the First Ministers. We are not trying to amend the whole Accord. We are not in any sense reducing the importance of the fundamental achievements that have been accomplished by the Accord. Indeed, we think these modest amendments would in fact enhance the Accord.
We have also suggested subjects for constitutional conferences to come. We have looked at the revoking of Section 33 of the Charter. That has to be revoked. The section allows the provinces and the federal Government, for that matter, to ignore the Charter for a five-year period on any particular legislation. It is crucial that it go in the next round of constitutional conferences.
We have also said that the changing nature of Canadian society, the increasing ethnoculture reality of today's society, should be an item of top priority on the agenda of the next Constitution conference. We have made several other suggestions, above all about the process of constitutional making. We must have input from the public through legislative committees, federal and provincial, and through public hearings, before First Ministers meet as well as after, and we continue to press that as hard as we possibly can.
We think, however, particularly in the light of some of the events that have taken place in the last month since we discussed Meech Lake, that a really very significant achievement was brought about. True, it was 11 men sitting around into late hours, but they did represent all the political Parties. They did discuss and debate the issues, although in private, on the basis of about 60 years of discussion of these matters, and intense discussion on the Quebec agenda for the previous two years.
I spent a weekend recently pretending that I was all 11 First Ministers, wondering if I could, as a woman, come up with a better constitutional Accord. With the exception of the amendments we have proposed, I had to come to the conclusion that this was really an historic achievement. The last time we had men sitting around doing something for us was the famous kitchen cabinet back in November of 1981, when three men arranged things to almost completely forget women and native people. That was about the worst example in my memory of people sitting around in a closed environment, a kitchen, in that case. If ever there needed to be a woman in the kitchen, it was certainly then. They came up with some pretty shocking anomalies and forgetfulness.
I do not think that has been the case this time, with the exception of some proposals on which we have made our amendments and which I have gone over today.
May 19, 1988

We should also look at the fact that not only did the premiers represent all the provinces and all political Parties, but also that the agreement that they reached at Meech Lake and then subsequently in finer print at the Langevin Block, was only the fourth time in Canadian history that unanimity among the partners has been reached on a constitutional amendment. Getting agreement on important constitutional change in Canada is about as rare as Haley's Comet. It happened in 1940 on unemployment insurance and it happened in 1951 and 1964 when concurrent jurisdiction over old age pensions was being achieved. Those are the only times we have achieved agreement in the last 50 years until the Meech Lake Constitutional Accord.
We have now seen four of the provinces approve the Accord. Two more provinces, probably four more, will have approved it through their legislatures by fall. After the hearings are completed in the Ontario Legislature, it is expected to go through. It will go through the New Brunswick Legislature after hearings have been held there. I understand they will begin in early September. I regret very much that the Government of Nova Scotia decided not to hold hearings. We have protested that vigorously. The Government of Nova Scotia has appeared to decide to present the matter to the legislature for approval without hearings. Saskatchewan held hearings and Manitoba will hold hearings.
One naturally wonders about two provinces. There has been great speculation about them as they have new premiers since the Accord was achieved. That is Manitoba and New Brunswick. As I just mentioned, they will both be holding hearings and as a result of those hearings, I hope they will be able to support the Accord. I found it quite incredible to be told by the Liberal Leader in Manitoba that Meech Lake was dead. I do not know how she can speak for members of the other two Parties. She has just over a third of the seats in the legislature and cannot simply proclaim Meech Lake is dead. I think members of the New Democratic Party would certainly not accept the Leader of the Liberal Party speaking for them, nor do I expect would the Conservative Members of the Manitoba Legislature.
It looks very much like the New Brunswick hearings will begin in September. British Columbia will be presenting a resolution very soon, as will Newfoundland. So the possibility of reaching provincial consent to the Accord, I think, is really very great. It surprises me all the more when I pick up the newspapers and read almost daily that Meech Lake is on the rocks, that it will not be approved and that it will have to go back entirely to the drawing board. That is certainly not the way I read the developments of the past four or five months.
I want to close by not only emphasizing what a historical achievement this has been, how rare it is that we can get agreement and how good, by and large, the agreement is, but also to point out that when we really start looking at all the potential changes in the agreement, any one can find probably 50. You can sit down and do it as I have done myself. Then one comes to the conclusion that very few of those changes
Constitution Amendment, 1987
that one can dream up to be made to the Meech Lake agreement are ones which would receive unanimous agreement.
I mentioned some time ago whether or not the First Ministers should not have minority language rights promoted as well as preserved. Indeed, the special joint committee recommended that that should be the case. However, I think I am safe in saying that in British Columbia, for example, it was a fairly major achievement to agree to preserve minority language rights. I am speaking in respect of it being a major achievement for Mr. Vander Zalm, the Premier of the province. It was a real step forward. Whether he would agree to go additionally to promote at this stage is doubtful. Preserve, as I pointed out earlier, can mean a very great deal.
Even the New Democrats in British Columbia in their suggested amendments to Meech Lake did not make that one. So when we pick out whatever proposal it is we will find that some provinces would agree with it, some groups in society would agree with it, others would disagree with it and others would not even put it on the agenda.
It is in the context of looking at all the proposals we have heard over the last several months, and the realization of how difficult it would be to put all these together in one package that would be acceptable, and in the context, too, as I have stressed in my remarks today, of the strength within the Meech Lake Accord itself, once we get over all the naysaying, that I-and I hope and trust I speak on behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party-recommend most warmly the adoption once again of the constitutional Accord by this House.

SIKH ORGANIZATIONS-MINISTER'S LETTER TO PREMIERS/POLICY OF DEPARTMENT

['We shall resume debate but do so very briefly.\nThe motion to ajourn the House is now deemed to have been adopted. Accordingly this House stands adjourned until tomorrow at 10 a.m., pursuant to Standing Order 3(1).']

Mr. Speaker, on April 18, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) questions regarding the advice he had gratuitously given provincial Premiers to boycott meetings organized in communities in their provinces by a number of Canadian Sikh organizations. I referred to the Babbar Khalsa, the International Sikh Youth Organization, and the World Sikh Organization.
The questions resulted from the fact that there was a gathering in Toronto organized by a variety of organizations.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs said that there were a number of temples involved. Others asserted that the three Sikh organizations had been among the sponsors of this event.
In responding to my question the Minister spoke of gatherings of moderate Sikhs which occur in various places. He mentioned a quite distinctive event in Edmonton organized to honour the Prairie Link newspaper where he said many moderate Sikhs had appeared. He then declared:
If we want Sikh communities in Canada to be governed by the moderates who want to live within the rules of Canada, a large part of our challenge is to be seen to be associated with those moderates.
In the case of the World Sikh Organization, in particular, representatives of which have been appearing before the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism, and whose members in fact have not been charged with terrorist activity-certainly they have not been found guilty of any such activity-I asked him what he had to say to the suggestion that his blanket charge in his letter to the Premiers reflected a deplorable attitude, that it expressed a matter of judging people long before they had been found guilty in any court of law. I suggested that he was opening possibilities of Sikhs being found guilty by association with organizations which themselves might, in the case of the World Sikh Organization, have a particular concern about the creation of a distinct state of Khalistan. But he said that it is doing so by peaceful means and not by any kind of violence or any kind of terrorism.
In response to this question the Minister declared:
There is a small minority within the Sikh community in Canada that is running not only against the rules of order of Canada but that is running against the preferences of the great majority of Canadians of Sikh origin. We cannot leave that great majority of Sikhs without support. We need to support them and we need to do it evidently. The Hon. Member needs to do it, I need to do it and my colleague needs to do it. That is what both she and I were doing this past weekend.
Let me say that the Minister and his Department have not been doing that "evidently". He has been adamant in his refusal to appear before the standing committee, or at least he was through to the meeting this morning. He is preoccupied with security considerations and with charges of terrorism against organizations and their members. The Government of Canada has in fact not followed the advice which the Minister himself was giving to us today.
The concern that I am expressing goes far beyond concern about a letter, three organizations, and advice given so gratuitously. The Department of External Affairs has intervened in all manner of areas relating to the Canadian Government and the Canadian Sikh community.
In discussions with the former Secretary of State, the now resigned the Member for Rosedale, Mr. Crombie, when I congratulated him in the House for having created the Chair for Sikh Studies and having provided funding from the federal Government to match community contributions, he alluded to
May 19, 1988

the pressure that had been put on by the Department of External Affairs and by the security agencies of this country in opposition to that.
The Federation of Sikh Societies of Canada, which ought to be that organization of moderate Sikhs if there is to be such a national organization, has been denied any funding for a couple of years. It has been forced into the basement of a Canadian Sikh because of lack of funds to carry on its endeavours.
As the Minister stated, if it were true that the Government of Canada was supporting those organizations against which no charges have ever been made, and if it were doing the correct thing for the Sikh community as a whole instead of expressing in one way and another the suspicion of Sikhs generally about what the Government of India wants these days, then I would have less reason to be here this afternoon protesting.
There are the most serious actions being taken by the Government of Canada in which the Secretary of State for External Affairs is a leader. Those actions destabilize the community, cause difficulties, and create a lack of harmony among the ethnocultural communities in Canada.
This is a most serious matter. I hope that whoever responds to this on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs might be equipped to take my message back to the Department, because I am very much afraid whatever I am going to be given in the next few moments will be some more claptrap and preoccupation with one small point, quite missing large national realities and multicultural issues of the most far-reaching significance to the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bud Bradley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we appreciate the concern of the Hon. Member, and I assure him that the Department will be advised of the new points he raised tonight.
It is important to stress at the outset that the letters sent by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to the Premiers were not directed at the entire Sikh community in Canada. The overwhelming majority of Sikhs in this country are responsible, law-abiding citizens. Indeed, the Sikh community has made an enormous and undeniable contribution to Canadian society since the beginning of the century.
It should also be noted that the Minister told the Premiers that it was his view that participation in Sikh community activity by members of Government was valuable for them, both in keeping abreast of the interests of the Sikh community and in encouraging that community to participate fully in Canadian life.
The letters of the Secretary of State for External Affairs referred only to three groups which exist largely or exclusively to promote the creation of an independent Sikh state in India known as Khalistan. Some members of some of these groups have advocated violent means to achieve their ends. It is the
Adjournment Debate
advocacy of violence which is of greatest concern. The Canadian Government cannot remain silent when individuals or organizations threaten violence to achieve the dismemberment of a country with which Canada has friendly relations. Hence, the Minister's letters asked provincial Premiers to do no more than avoid appearing at events and activities organized by those groups.
It was not suggested that politicians avoid receiving or meeting with any individuals, no matter what views they may espouse. It is the attendance or participation in events or functions sponsored by those three organizations which is of concern. When political leaders openly associate with such groups, whether they intend to or not, they lend credence and support to the objectives for which those organizations stand. Moreover, those organizations have taken advantage of politicians attending their functions, for example, by having them photographed under the "Khalistan" flag.
If the situation were reversed, most Canadians would strongly object, as would the Canadian Government, to leaders of other countries giving support to anyone who promoted the dismemberment of Canada, particularly through violent means. In such circumstances Canada would certainly seek to have the Government of that country not give or be seen to give, any type of support to such activities.
Finally, the Secretary of State for External Affairs is responsible for developing foreign policies which benefit all Canadians, as well as for providing advice and guidance on those policies. It would be an abdication of those responsibilities if the Minister were simply to ignore a matter which has serious foreign policy implications for Canada's relations with a friendly Government such as India on an issue which it regards as being vital to its national survival.
FISHERIES-REPORTED SPILL OF SULPHURIC ACID INTO STRAITS OF GEORGIA/PREVENTIVE MEASURES TO CONTAIN EFFLUENT

Mr. Speaker, I wish to elaborate on a matter that was raised in the House some time ago. It concerned an environmental spill in the Strait of Georgia from the Crown Forest Products operation outside Campbell River. The matter involved the spill of approximately 30 tonnes of 97 per cent sulphuric acid into the Strait of Georgia. The matter was not reported.
There are several things which can be learned from this experience. The first thing is that the matter was reported some time later by employees of the operation to the provincial Ministry of the Environment, to the federal Ministry of the Environment, and to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
In the subsequent examination of this matter the people at Fisheries and Oceans who examined the question did not report back to the employees. There is a very energetic environmental committee in that operation, and to date they have had some less than exciting results in attempting to relate to management on important matters of environmental concern in that pulp and paper operation. It is incumbent upon

May 19, 1988
Adjournment Debate
the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, the Department of the Environment, and all federal government Departments concerned with enforcing environmental matters, that they recognize and respect employee environmental committees. After all, this is an important source of information.
It is my hope that there will be a recognition and a statement by the Minister that, any time a matter is reported by an individual or an organized group concerned about the environment, not only the company will be consulted about the matter but indeed the employee environmental committees will be contacted, briefed on the findings, and encouraged at any point to report any further concerns they may have.
There are environmental committees working in a large number of pulp mills on the coast of British Columbia. They provide a very important service to the employees who work in the pulp and paper industry and in the specific operations. In fact, they provide a service to the management and owners of those operations, as well as to the people who live in the area and who are concerned about the environment.
It is my hope that the Minister will not overlook this, that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) will write to the chairperson of the environmental committee of the Crown Forest Operation in Campbell River, and that indeed regional officials will brief that committee on the outcome of the examination of the spill and will work closely with it in their future endeavours to make the environment in that area safer and cleaner.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bud Bradley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter of an acid spill in British Columbia at the Crown Forest pulp mill near Campbell River was raised in the House some three weeks ago. I would like to take this opportunity to outline our understanding of the spill and the steps taken by officials of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans in response to the incident. I might also add that officials of Environment Canada co-operated with DFO in a joint review of the spill.
As the matter is currently being investigated under the authority of the federal Fisheries Act, I am sure Members will appreciate that, in order not to jeopardize the investigation, only a overview of the incident can be presented at this time.
Information that a spill of acid had occurred at the Crown Forest Ltd. pulp mill near Campbell River, B.C. was first brought to the attention of DFO on April 20, 1988. This information was passed on to the Department by a concerned mill employee. Details of this spill were provided to officials of the Province of B.C. by the company on April 22, 1988. The brief summary I will give you now is based principally on those details provided by the company.
On March 25, 1988 sulphuric acid spilled or, as the company prefers to indicate, "leaked" into a sewer over about a three-hour period. This loss of acid apparently occurred
following repairs to a pump in the mill when a pump drain was left open allowing the acid to escape into the mill's effluent sewer system. The acid flowed from the mill's sewer system into the marine environment through an underwater mill effluent diffuser in Discovery Passage, part of the Straits of Georgia.
The company has estimated the loss of acid to be approximately 31 tons or 3,700 gallons. The company concluded that this acid, which was discharged over a three-hour period, along with regular mill effluent through its effluent diffuser, would not have any environmental impact. For this reason the company did not consider it necessary to report this spill immediately either to provincial or federal authorities. However, to prevent the recurrence of similar incidents, the company has reviewed operating procedures in the mill and is considering the installation of a pH alarm system in its control room and another alarm system within the mill where the leak occurred to detect leaks anywhere in the acid storage area.
As I mentioned earlier, Mr. Speaker, federal officials were not notified of the incident until almost one month after the event. Because of this significant delay, an environmental impact assessment of the spill could not be carried out. Nonetheless, an investigation of the incident was conducted by both DFO and Environment Canada. DFO has asked Environment Canada to review the spill reporting procedures at this mill to determine if procedures or works, additional to those proposed by the company, are required to prevent future spills and to ensure proper spill reporting. I am pleased to report that the company has now agreed to report all spills of this nature in the future.
I would like to assure this House that the Department takes seriously all spills of hazardous chemicals that might occur not only at pulp mills but also at other industrial facilities. For this reason DFO, in concert with Environment Canada and provincial authorities, will continue to respond to and investigate spill events that could affect fishery resources and take appropriate action in response to such spills.
I would also at this time like to thank my colleague for the further information and points that he has raised this evening. I can assure my hon. colleague that the Minister will be advised of his points, and a response will be given on what action the Minister deems necessary.
